text: Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. It is for them alone to point out what we ought to do, as well as to determine what we shall do.
context_note: The opening sentences of Bentham's system: pleasure and pain are both the explanation of conduct and the standard for judging it — the foundation every utilitarian argument builds on.

text: all punishment is mischief: all punishment in itself is evil. Upon the principle of utility, if it ought at all to be admitted, it ought only to be admitted in as far as it promises to exclude some greater evil.
context_note: Punishment must earn its keep in prevented suffering — the frame within which Bentham attacked the death penalty as unprofitable, irremissible mischief.

text: The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?
context_note: Bentham's footnote that redrew the boundary of moral concern at sentience — the founding text of the animal-welfare tradition in ethics.

text: The creed which accepts as the foundation of morals, Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness.
context_note: Mill's canonical statement of the principle, with happiness understood as pleasure and the absence of pain — refined in the same chapter by the doctrine of higher pleasures.

Mill's answer to 'useful lies': the institution of trustworthy assertion is itself among the greatest utilities, so each convenient lie spends a common inheritance. Exceptions exist and should themselves be rule-governed.

text: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
context_note: The higher-pleasures doctrine in its famous epigram: utilitarian contentment is not complacency, and some discontent is the price of capacities worth having.

text: the sentiment of justice appears to me to be, the animal desire to repel or retaliate a hurt or damage to oneself, or to those with whom one sympathizes, widened so as to include all persons, by the human capacity of enlarged sympathy, and the human conception of intelligent self-interest.
context_note: Resentment naturalized and moralized: the retaliatory impulse becomes the sentiment of justice only when widened to all persons — anger disciplined by impartiality.

text: the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.
context_note: The harm principle: self-regarding conduct lies outside legitimate coercion. Mill grounds it not in natural right but in the long-run utility of liberty.

text: Drunkenness, for example, in ordinary cases, is not a fit subject for legislative interference; but I should deem it perfectly legitimate that a person, who had once been convicted of any act of violence to others under the influence of drink, should be placed under a special legal restriction, personal to himself;
context_note: Mill's worked example: intoxication as such is self-regarding, but the drinker with a record of drunken violence has made his drinking other-regarding — the harm principle drawing its line case by case.

text: We have a right, also, in various ways, to act upon our unfavourable opinion of any one, not to the oppression of his individuality, but in the exercise of ours.
context_note: Judgment of others is licensed — avoidance, warning, withheld company — but bounded: natural consequences of opinion, never punishment for self-regarding conduct.

text: War is an ugly thing, but not the ugliest of things: the decayed and degraded state of moral and patriotic feeling which thinks that nothing is worth war, is much worse.
context_note: Written during the American Civil War: Mill weighs war's evils against the evils war can end (he had slavery in view) — consequentialist war ethics in one sentence.

text: Marriage is the only actual bondage known to our law. There remain no legal slaves, except the mistress of every house.
context_note: Mill's indictment of Victorian marriage law: where exit is barred and rights unequal, marriage functions as bondage. The reform case for lawful divorce is utilitarian to its core — suffering trapped is suffering multiplied.

text: no man of ripe years and of sound mind, acting freely, and with his eyes open, ought to be hindered, with a view to his advantage, from making such bargain, in the way of obtaining money, as he thinks fit:
context_note: Bentham against the usury laws — and against his teacher Adam Smith: consenting adults' credit bargains are presumptively utility-increasing, and rate caps chiefly starve the risky borrower into worse hands.

text: With what chance of success, for example, would a legislator go about to extirpate drunkenness and fornication by dint of legal punishment?
context_note: From Bentham's chapter on the limits of the penal branch of jurisprudence: conduct that private ethics may condemn can still lie beyond profitable legislation, because the punishment needed would cost more suffering than the practice it suppresses.

text: Human beings owe to each other help to distinguish the better from the worse, and encouragement to choose the former and avoid the latter.
context_note: Mill's answer to the charge that his doctrine counsels selfish indifference: refusing to coerce a neighbour is not refusing to counsel, remonstrate with, or think ill of him — persuasion is owed precisely because compulsion is not.

text: Protection, therefore, against the tyranny of the magistrate is not enough: there needs protection also against the tyranny of the prevailing opinion and feeling; against the tendency of society to impose, by other means than civil penalties, its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them;
context_note: Mill's warning that collective disapproval can coerce as thoroughly as law and with fewer checks; it marks the point at which everyday moral judgment of others turns into a social penalty.

text: Every one who receives the protection of society owes a return for the benefit, and the fact of living in society renders it indispensable that each should be bound to observe a certain line of conduct towards the rest.
context_note: The opening of Mill's chapter on the authority of society: the argument that limits interference with self-regarding conduct also grounds genuine civic obligation — bearing one's share of the burdens that protect everyone.

text: The only freedom which deserves the name, is that of pursuing our own good in our own way, so long as we do not attempt to deprive others of theirs, or impede their efforts to obtain it.
context_note: Mill's statement of the liberty the harm principle protects. Where law or custom crosses that boundary, the utilitarian case for compliance is weakened rather than reinforced by the same reasoning that recommends obedience elsewhere.

text: An opinion that corn-dealers are starvers of the poor, or that private property is robbery, ought to be unmolested when simply circulated through the press, but may justly incur punishment when delivered orally to an excited mob assembled before the house of a corn-dealer,
context_note: Mill's worked example that words are judged by their circumstances and effects: the identical proposition is protected in print and blamable when it becomes an instigation before an angry crowd.

text: the peculiar evil of silencing the expression of an opinion is, that it is robbing the human race; posterity as well as the existing generation; those who dissent from the opinion, still more than those who hold it.
context_note: Mill grounds free discussion in utility rather than right: suppression costs everyone the chance to exchange error for truth, or to hold a true belief for living reasons. Restraints on speech therefore have to be argued for, not assumed.

text: Undoubtedly the manner of asserting an opinion, even though it be a true one, may be very objectionable, and may justly incur severe censure.
context_note: Having defended the freest expression of opinion, Mill immediately concedes that how a thing is said — invective, stigmatising opponents as bad men — can itself deserve blame, though he doubts such offences can safely be handed to law.
